procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated April 29, 1965 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Misc. Contempt Case No. 43 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Mahabir filed a petition under Art. 227 in the High Court and obtained a stay of the proceedings on December 20, 1963. The High Court admitted the application and stayed further proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by special leave from the Allahabad High Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and order of the High Court.

directions: The judgment and order of the High Court is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Panchayat is guilty of contempt of court for continuing a trial after being informed of a High Court stay order, when the application was not supported by a proper affidavit or other evidence, and whether the Panchayat was bound to adjourn the proceedings for better proof.

facts: An accused person (M) in a case before a Panchayat informed them that the High Court had issued an order staying the proceedings.
To support this claim, M filed an application with a document purporting to be an affidavit.
However, this document was not a proper affidavit as it had not been sworn before a person authorized to administer oaths.
The application also lacked crucial details, such as the date of the alleged stay order, and did not include a copy of a telegram from M's lawyer that was mentioned.
The Panchayat, disbelieving M's claim due to the lack of proper evidence, continued with the trial and convicted him.
The High Court later found the Panchayat members guilty of contempt, stating they should have adjourned the proceedings to allow M to produce a certified copy of the order.
law: To establish contempt of court for disobeying an order, it must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the person had knowledge of the order. Any doubt benefits the person charged.
A judicial officer is not legally bound to adjourn proceedings to allow a party to obtain better proof of a claim.
A finding of contempt against a judicial officer requires "unimpeachable evidence" that they knew of the higher court's order and deliberately disobeyed it.
Panchas are not expected to be as well-versed in law and procedure as ordinary courts, and their actions should be judged with this in mind.
application: The Supreme Court found that the material presented to the Panchayat was extremely weak. The "so-called affidavit" was not a legal affidavit, and the application lacked essential information.
Given the insufficient evidence, the Court concluded that the Panchayat's decision to disbelieve the accused's mere statement was made in good faith (bona fide).
The Court held that the Panchayat was not obligated to adjourn the case. The decision to adjourn was within their discretion, and their refusal to do so in good faith did not amount to contempt.
The standard of proof for contempt had not been met, as there was no unimpeachable evidence that the Panchas actually knew about the stay order and willfully disobeyed it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, ruling that the Panchayat was not guilty of contempt of court. The Court reasoned that the Panchayat acted in good faith by refusing to halt proceedings based on an application that was not supported by a proper affidavit or any other credible evidence of the High Court's stay order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Panchayat is guilty of contempt of court for continuing a trial after being informed of a High Court stay order, when the application was not supported by a proper affidavit or other evidence, and whether the Panchayat was bound to adjourn the proceedings for better proof.
appellant_arguments: No contempt of court was established because a court is entitled to not act on an application that is not accompanied by a properly sworn affidavit or a certified copy of the order.
Even if the Panchas erred in not staying the proceedings, it must be definitively proven that they acted deliberately to bypass the High Court's order to be found guilty of contempt.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not re-appreciate the facts of the case as determined by the High Court.

cases.principle: To justify committal for breach of a prohibitive order, it is not necessary for the order to have been formally served. It is sufficient if it is proven that the person had notice of the order through other means ('aliunde'), such as a telegram or newspaper report, and knew it was intended to be enforced.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To hold a person in contempt for disobeying a court order, it must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt that they had knowledge of the order. A person cannot be held guilty of contempt if they bona fide conclude, based on the material before them, that the source of information regarding the order is not authentic. The benefit of any doubt regarding knowledge must be given to the person charged.
obiter: In order to justify committal for breach of a prohibitive order it is not necessary that the order should have been served upon the party against whom it has been granted, if it be proved that he had notice of the order aliunde.
We need not consider whether it makes any difference in law if the order has been drawn up.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A court or judicial body, like a Panchayat, cannot be held guilty of contempt for proceeding with a case after being informed of a stay order if the information is presented without authentic proof. If the judicial body forms a bona fide conclusion that the information is unreliable due to the lack of a proper affidavit or other evidence, its refusal to stay the proceedings does not amount to wilful disobedience of the higher court's order.
legal_tests_applied: To establish contempt of court for disobeying an order, the party making the assertion must prove beyond all reasonable doubt that the person had knowledge of the order.
If there is any doubt as to whether the person had knowledge of the order, the benefit of the doubt must be given to the person charged with contempt.

If a person bona fide concludes on the material placed before him that the source of information about an order is not authentic, he cannot be held guilty of contempt of court for disobeying the order.
why_respondent_won: The application informing the Panchayat of the stay order was not supported by an affidavit sworn before a person authorized to administer oaths.
The application lacked crucial details, such as the date of the High Court's order, and was not accompanied by any supporting evidence like a copy of the alleged telegram from the advocate.
Given the insufficient and unverified material, the Panchayat's bona fides could not be doubted when they refused to accept the mere statement of a party that proceedings had been stayed.

A judicial officer is not bound to adjourn proceedings to allow a party to furnish better proof of a stay order; if the officer, acting in good faith, chooses not to grant an adjournment, this discretionary act cannot be considered contempt of court.
policy_considerations: The standard of proof for contempt of court is high ('beyond all reasonable doubt') and any doubt must be resolved in favor of the accused, ensuring that individuals are not punished for contempt without clear and convincing evidence of wilful disobedience.
